lead: A square matrix A turns most vectors into vectors pointing in a new direction. A few special vectors keep their line: A only scales them. That scale factor is an eigenvalue and the vector is an eigenvector. The equation Ax = λx hunts for these directions, and it collapses into a polynomial equation, det(A − λI) = 0, whose roots are the eigenvalues. Engineers use them to find vibration frequencies, search engines use the dominant one to rank pages, and data analysts use them to compress features. This chapter shows how to compute them by hand.
prereq: You need: determinants and the meaning of a singular matrix from Unit 1 (Matrices and Systems of Linear Equations), and null space and basis from Unit 2 (Vector Spaces).

blocks.text: Take a square matrix A of order n, with real or complex entries. Multiply A by a column vector x of length n and you get another vector Ax. Most choices of x come out tilted. Some do not.
Definition. A scalar λ is an eigenvalue of A if there is a nonzero vector x with Ax = λx. Such an x is an eigenvector of A belonging to λ.
Read the equation as a sentence: transforming x by the matrix A gives the same vector as scaling x by the number λ. The direction survives; the length changes by |λ|.
x must be nonzero. The zero vector obeys A0 = λ0 for every λ, so it carries no information, and the definition excludes it.

items: λ = 1: x is untouched, a fixed direction.
λ = 0: A sends a nonzero vector to 0, so A is singular and has no inverse.
λ negative: the arrow reverses. |λ| > 1 stretches, |λ| < 1 shrinks.

blocks.text: For a diagonal matrix the standard basis vectors are eigenvectors. For A = diag(2, 3), A(1, 0) = (2, 0) = 2(1, 0) and A(0, 1) = (0, 3) = 3(0, 1), so 2 and 3 are the eigenvalues.

Some syllabi call eigenvalues latent roots and eigenvectors latent vectors; latent means hidden. The meaning is identical. A real matrix may have complex eigenvalues; only over C is every matrix guaranteed n eigenvalues.

sections.h3: The characteristic polynomial and characteristic equation

blocks.text: Start from Ax = λx with x ≠ 0. Write λx as λIx, where I is the n×n identity matrix. Then (A − λI)x = 0.

This is a homogeneous system whose coefficient matrix is A − λI. It has a nonzero solution exactly when that matrix is singular, because singular matrices have a null space larger than {0} (Unit 1 and Unit 2). So λ is an eigenvalue exactly when det(A − λI) = 0.
p(λ) = det(A − λI) = (−1)<sup>n</sup>λ<sup>n</sup> + c<sub>n−1</sub>λ<sup>n−1</sup> + ⋯ + det A
blocks.where: p(λ) is the characteristic polynomial of A; λ is a scalar variable; I is the identity matrix of order n; c<sub>n−1</sub> is some number built from the entries of A; det A is the constant term.

blocks.text: p is a polynomial of degree n. The equation det(A − λI) = 0 is the characteristic equation; its roots are exactly the eigenvalues, and over C there are n of them counted with multiplicity.

Sign convention. Some books use det(λI − A). That polynomial is (−1)n times the one above. The roots do not change; only the overall sign flips. Pick one convention and stay with it. This chapter uses det(A − λI).
Algebraic multiplicity. If λ₀ is a root repeated k times, then k is its algebraic multiplicity. A root that occurs once has multiplicity 1.

Two shortcuts. For 2×2 A, det(A − λI) = λ² − (trace A)λ + det A. For a triangular matrix, A − λI is also triangular, so its determinant is (a₁₁ − λ)(a₂₂ − λ)⋯(a<sub>nn</sub> − λ): the eigenvalues are just the diagonal entries, each repeated as often as it appears.
Fix one eigenvalue λ. Its eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors in the null space of A − λI. That null space is a subspace called the eigenspace of A for λ, written Eλ.

items: Subtract λ from every diagonal entry of A to get A − λI.
Row reduce A − λI. Never try to invert it; it is singular by construction.
Solve (A − λI)x = 0 in terms of the free variables; each free variable gives a basis vector of E<sub>λ</sub>.
Keep the nonzero vectors only, and check one: compute Ax and λx and confirm they match.

blocks.text: The dimension of Eλ is the geometric multiplicity of λ. It is at least 1 and never exceeds the algebraic multiplicity. The gap between the two decides diagonalization; see 4.2 and 4.4.

3×3 example. A = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 1], [0, 0, 2]] is upper triangular, so p(λ) = (1 − λ)(2 − λ)² and the eigenvalues are 1 (multiplicity 1) and 2 (multiplicity 2). For λ = 2, A − 2I = [[−1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0]], giving −x₁ = 0 and x₃ = 0 with x₂ free. So E₂ is spanned by (0, 1, 0): one dimension against algebraic multiplicity 2.
Complex case. For R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]], det(R − λI) = λ² + 1, so λ = ±i. Over R there is no eigenvalue. Over C, R(1, −i) = (i, 1) = i(1, −i), so (1, −i) belongs to i.

figure.caption: Follow the chain for the worked example A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]: the determinant gives λ² − 7λ + 10, whose roots 5 and 2 each open a null space of eigenvectors.

spec.title: Eigenvalue flow
spec.aria: A flow from matrix A to A minus lambda I, then the characteristic equation, then eigenvalues, then the null space, then nonzero eigenvectors.

examples.question: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], find the characteristic polynomial, both eigenvalues, and one eigenvector for each eigenvalue. Verify each eigenvector.
steps: Take the determinant: (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − (1)(2) = 12 − 4λ − 3λ + λ² − 2 = λ² − 7λ + 10.
Solve λ² − 7λ + 10 = 0. The discriminant is 49 − 40 = 9, so λ = (7 ± 3)/2, giving λ = 5 and λ = 2.
Cross-check with the shortcuts: trace = 4 + 3 = 7 = 5 + 2, and det = 12 − 2 = 10 = 5 × 2. Both match.
For λ = 5: A − 5I = [[−1, 1], [2, −2]]. Row reduction gives the single equation −x₁ + x₂ = 0, so x₂ = x₁. Choose x = (1, 1).
For λ = 2: A − 2I = [[2, 1], [2, 1]]. Row reduction gives 2x₁ + x₂ = 0, so x₂ = −2x₁. Choose x = (1, −2).
The two eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, −2) are not multiples of each other, so together they span R².
examples.answer: The characteristic polynomial is λ² − 7λ + 10, the eigenvalues are λ = 5 and λ = 2, and eigenvectors are (1, 1) for λ = 5 and (1, −2) for λ = 2.
examples.check:
import math
A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]
tr = A[0][0] + A[1][1]
det = A[0][0] * A[1][1] - A[0][1] * A[1][0]
disc = tr * tr - 4 * det
l1 = (tr + math.sqrt(disc)) / 2
l2 = (tr - math.sqrt(disc)) / 2
print(int(tr))
print(int(det))
print(int(round(l1)))
print(int(round(l2)))

traps: The zero vector is never an eigenvector. It satisfies Ax = λx for every λ, so writing x = 0 as an answer loses marks.
Find λ first, then substitute that λ back into A − λI. Do not guess an eigenvector without verifying Ax = λx.
Sign convention: det(λI − A) gives (−1)ⁿ times the polynomial from det(A − λI). The roots are the same. If the question fixes a convention, do not swap it halfway.
A real matrix with a negative discriminant has complex eigenvalues. Write λ = ±i style answers over C; do not claim the matrix has no eigenvalues unless the field is stated as R.
Algebraic multiplicity is not the number of independent eigenvectors. For [[2, 1], [0, 2]] the eigenvalue 2 has multiplicity 2 but its eigenspace has dimension 1.

quiz.q: State the definitions of eigenvalue and eigenvector of a square matrix A.
quiz.a: λ is an eigenvalue if Ax = λx for some nonzero vector x; that x is an eigenvector belonging to λ.

quiz.q: Why does a nonzero eigenvector exist only when det(A − λI) = 0?
quiz.a: Ax = λx is the same as (A − λI)x = 0, a homogeneous system. A homogeneous system has a nonzero solution exactly when its coefficient matrix is singular, that is, when the determinant is zero.

quiz.q: For a 2×2 matrix A, write the characteristic polynomial in terms of trace and determinant, and explain where each coefficient comes from.
quiz.a: p(λ) = λ² − (trace A)λ + det A. The sum of the roots equals the trace and the product equals the determinant, matching the coefficients of the expanded polynomial.

quiz.q: Find the eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each of A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]].
Find the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] over C, and state what happens over R.
quiz.a: det(R − λI) = λ² + 1, so λ = i and λ = −i. Over C, E<sub>i</sub> is spanned by (1, −i) and E<sub>−i</sub> by (1, i). Over R there is no eigenvalue, since no real λ satisfies λ² + 1 = 0.

quiz.q: A is upper triangular of order 3 with diagonal entries 1, 2, 2, and the eigenspace for 2 has dimension 1. Explain what this tells you about the eigenvalues and about diagonalizing A.
quiz.a: The eigenvalues are 1, 2, 2 with algebraic multiplicities 1, 2, 2. Only one independent eigenvector belongs to 2, so the total count of independent eigenvectors is 2, less than 3. There is no basis of eigenvectors, so A is not diagonalizable; see 4.4.

quiz.q: Show that 0 is an eigenvalue of A if and only if A is singular.
quiz.a: If 0 is an eigenvalue, some nonzero x has Ax = 0x = 0, so the null space of A is larger than {0} and A is singular. Conversely, if A is singular, some nonzero x satisfies Ax = 0 = 0x, so 0 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector x.

beyond: Not for the exam. Nobody factors a degree-50 polynomial to find eigenvalues in practice; software uses iterative methods such as the QR algorithm, and power iteration to get the largest eigenvalue, inverse iteration the smallest. Google's PageRank is the dominant eigenvector of a huge link matrix, and principal component analysis is an eigenvector hunt on a covariance matrix. Control engineers read eigenvalues as stability, since a system settles only if all of them have negative real part. Search for power iteration, QR algorithm, spectral clustering, and the eigenvalues of a graph Laplacian.
